skill.name: When an author bends the usual structure
skill.why: Authors bend the usual shape on purpose. Spotting it shows you what they want.
skill.how: Know the usual shape. Spot what changed. Ask what the change does.

steps.say: Instructions usually just list the steps. I wrote teeth-brushing steps for the Preps, in a new way!

show.text: First, I wet you under the tap.
show.nudge: That's a step, in order. Instructions always have those. What's unusual?

show.text: Then I add a pea of paste.
show.nudge: Another step. Find the part instructions don't usually have.

steps.ask: Tap the part instructions don't usually have.
steps.win: Yes! Instructions don't start with 'Dear'. I kept the steps but bent the shape into a letter.

steps.say: Authors bend a shape on purpose. So I always ask: why?
steps.ask: Why write the steps as a letter for the Preps?

options.text: Because I forgot some steps.
options.reason: The steps are all there, in order. Authors bend shapes on purpose.

options.text: To make the steps fun, so Preps remember them.
To hide the steps from readers.
options.reason: Every step is still there. What does a letter add?

steps.win: Yes! A fun shape helps little kids remember. The job stays the same: brush your teeth.

creature.name: Topsittle
creature.blurb: A varied sittella that runs down tree trunks head first while other birds climb up. It knows the usual way, and bends it on purpose.

encounters.frame: A Topsittle dropped a note on the hut table. It's Wren's pancake recipe.
encounters.text:
Recipes usually start with a list of what you need. Then they give the steps. Wren wrote her pancake recipe as something else.

Dear Pancake,
First, I will find you a cup of flour, one egg and some milk. Then I will mix you in a bowl until you are smooth. Next, I will pour you into a hot pan. When you bubble, I will flip you over. Then I will eat you with lemon and sugar. Sorry about that.
Love, Wren
encounters.prompt: How did Wren bend the usual shape of a recipe?
encounters.success: She wrote it as a letter. It starts 'Dear Pancake' and ends 'Love, Wren', but the steps are all there.

options.text: She put the steps in the wrong order, from last to first.
options.reason: The steps are in the right order: mix, pour, flip, eat.

options.text: She wrote it as a letter to the pancake.
She left out the things you need.
options.reason: Flour, an egg and milk are all there, in the first step.

encounters.frame: Tully is telling the Topsittle about the grand final. She's telling it her own way.
encounters.text:
Stories usually go from the start to the finish. Tully told this one backwards.

The Snowcats lifted the cup. The crowd went wild. It was the best day of Tully's life. Just before that, Tully kicked the winning goal. A minute earlier, Zed had passed her the ball. At the start of the last quarter, the Snowcats were losing by five points. Nobody thought they could win. The Rams were already singing their team song.

items: The Snowcats were losing by five points.
body.reason: Start with the earliest thing: the last quarter began with the Snowcats losing. The cup comes last.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a guide to his favourite game. The Topsittle read it twice.
encounters.text:
Instructions usually use numbered steps and bossy words like press, jump and run. Zed wrote his game guide like this:

Once upon a time, a goat named Pip stood at the bottom of a mountain. First, she pressed the jump button and leapt onto a rock. Next, she ran past the sleepy yeti. Then she grabbed the golden carrot. At last, she reached the top, and everyone cheered. The end.

encounters.success: He told them as a story. It starts 'Once upon a time', but the steps are still in order.

options.reason: There's nothing to buy. It's a story that starts 'Once upon a time'.

options.reason: The steps are all there: jump, run past the yeti, grab the carrot.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote a spooky story for the hut logbook. The Topsittle read it with the lights on.
encounters.text:
Stories usually begin at the beginning. Wren's spooky story doesn't.

I should never have opened the door of the old hut on Crag Tower. That's how this story ends, so you might as well know it now. Here's how it began. On Tuesday night, Zed and I heard scratching from inside the hut. Then a thump. Then a long, low groan. Zed wanted to run. I wanted to know. We crept up the ladder in the dark, one rung at a time. The groaning got louder. My hand shook as I reached for the handle. I pulled the door open, and forty-three possums poured out over my boots, chattering and squeaking. Every one of them smelled terrible. My beanie still smells of possum.
encounters.prompt: Why might Wren start her story with the ending?
encounters.success: Starting with 'I should never have opened the door' makes you desperate to find out why.

options.text: So readers know they can skip the rest of the story.
options.reason: Starting with the end makes you keep reading to find out how it happened.

options.text: To make readers wonder what was behind the door.
Because she forgot how the story began.
options.reason: She tells the beginning straight after: 'Here's how it began.'

encounters.frame: Wren looked after a baby magpie for a week. The Topsittle read her diary.
encounters.text:
Diaries usually start with the first day and end with the last. Wren's diary goes backwards.

Friday: The baby magpie flew away today. I cried a bit. Then I cleaned out its box.
Thursday: It flew all the way across the hut and landed on Mo's head. Mo screamed. Then he laughed.
Wednesday: It flapped its wings for the first time and fell off the table. Gus said that's how all great flyers start.
Tuesday: It ate six worms and a bit of Gus's sandwich.
Monday: I found a baby magpie under a snow gum. It couldn't fly, so I took it back to the hut. I named it Pickle.
encounters.prompt: Put the events in the order they really happened.
encounters.success: Found, fed, flapped, flew, gone. Reading it backwards makes the goodbye come first.

items: Wren found a baby magpie that couldn't fly.
The magpie ate six worms and some of Gus's sandwich.
The magpie flapped its wings and fell off the table.
The magpie flew across the hut and landed on Mo's head.
The magpie flew away, and Wren cleaned out its box.
body.reason: The diary starts on Friday. The real story starts on Monday, when Wren found the magpie.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote art instructions for the little kids at base camp. The Topsittle loved them.
encounters.text:
Art instructions usually list what you need, then give the steps. Indi wrote hers as a fairy tale.

You will need: a paintbrush, a sheet of paper, a pot of blue paint and a cup of water.

Once upon a time, a lonely paintbrush lived in a jar. One day, a girl took it out and gave it three friends: the paper, the paint and the water. 'First, dip me in the water,' said the brush. 'Next, dip me in the paint.' The girl did as she was told. 'Now sweep me across the paper, from side to side.' A sky appeared. 'Last of all, wash me clean,' said the brush, 'and put me back in my jar.' And the paintbrush and the sky lived happily ever after.
encounters.prompt: Sort these. What stayed the same as usual instructions, and what did Indi change?
encounters.success: The list and the steps in order stayed. Indi changed the rest into a fairy tale with a talking brush.

items.text: The steps are in order: water, paint, sweep, wash.
items.reason: Usual instructions give steps in order, and Indi's still do.

items.text: The story part begins with 'Once upon a time'.
items.reason: Instructions don't usually tell a story. Indi changed that.

items.text: A list at the top says what you need.
items.reason: Usual instructions list what you need first. Indi kept her list at the top.

items.text: The paintbrush is a character who talks.
items.reason: In usual instructions, nobody talks. Indi made the brush give the steps.

items.text: It ends with 'happily ever after'.
items.reason: That's a fairy tale ending. Usual instructions just stop after the last step.

encounters.frame: A bottle washed up below Scaffold Peaks. The Topsittle pulled out the paper inside.
encounters.text:
Reports about animals usually give facts, with headings like 'Size' and 'Food'. This one arrived in a bottle.

Dear humans,
Greetings from the warm, blue ocean! I'm a whale shark. I'm the biggest fish in the sea, about as long as a bus, but don't worry. I only eat tiny plankton. I swim along with my huge mouth open and gulp them down. My skin is covered in white spots, and no two whale sharks have the same pattern. I can live for more than a hundred years. Divers say I'm gentle, and they're right. I let them swim right beside me. Wish you were here!
P.S. Please stop dropping plastic in my ocean. It tastes terrible.
Love,
Wally the Whale Shark

encounters.success: It's a letter from the whale shark. The facts are all there, told by the animal itself.

options.reason: The facts are there: its size, its food, its spots and how long it lives.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote the match report for the Scaffold Peaks Gazette. The Topsittle thinks it smells delicious.
encounters.text:
RECIPE FOR A COMEBACK
Serves: one very happy footy club.
Ingredients: eighteen tired Snowcats, one slippery ball, a thirty-point deficit at half-time and one coach with a very loud voice.
Method:
1. Take your tired Snowcats and leave them in a freezing change room for twenty minutes, while the coach shouts.
2. Stir in three quick goals at the start of the third quarter.
3. Add a mark on the siren by a nervous full-forward.
4. Let him kick it straight through the middle.
5. Serve hot: Snowcats 64, Rams 62.
Chef's tip: Do not panic if your mixture looks flat at half-time. Ours did, and it rose beautifully.

That, Snowcats fans, is how you cook up a comeback. Next week's recipe: a grand final win, served with extra gravy.
encounters.prompt: Why might Tully have written her match report as a recipe?
encounters.success: A recipe is a set of steps that build something. Tully shows the comeback was built the same way.

options.text: To teach readers how to bake a cake for the footy club's party.
options.reason: Nothing here can be baked. The 'ingredients' are players, a ball and a losing score.

options.text: To keep the final score a secret from the Rams supporters.
options.reason: The score is right there in step 5: Snowcats 64, Rams 62.

options.text: To show the win was built step by step, like cooking a dish.
Because the team went out for dinner after the match.
options.reason: The report never mentions dinner. The recipe is just a way to tell the match.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a story about the Frost Cup final. The Topsittle mixed up his notes.
encounters.text: The screen went white, and the crowd in the library gasped. Zed's character was frozen solid, one jump from the finish line. For a moment, the library was so quiet that you could hear the snow falling outside. Ten minutes earlier, everything had been fine. Zed had won the first two rounds easily, and his rival, Kit, had looked worried. Then, in round three, Kit had found a secret ice cannon behind a waterfall. She had waited until Zed was right at the edge of the last cliff before firing it. Now, frozen, Zed could only watch as Kit strolled past and crossed the line. He took a deep breath, shook her hand and asked her to show him the waterfall. Kit said yes, but only if Zed promised never to use it on her. Everyone agreed it was the best final the library had ever seen.
encounters.prompt: Zed's story doesn't start at the beginning. Why might he start with the freeze?
encounters.success: Starting at the most exciting moment grabs readers. Then they want to know how Zed ended up frozen.

options.text: To grab readers with the most exciting moment, then show how it happened.
Because the start of the final was too boring to write about.
options.reason: The start is still told, straight after. Zed held it back, he didn't cut it.

options.text: To hide who won the Frost Cup until the very last line.
options.reason: Kit crosses the line soon after the freeze. The winner isn't hidden.

options.text: Because every good story has to start in the middle.
options.reason: Most stories start at the start. Zed bent the order on purpose, for this one.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote an echidna report for the ranger station. The Topsittle thinks it's prickly.
encounters.text:
THE SPIKY TRUTH: An interview with Edna the Echidna
Q: Edna, thanks for joining us. What's with the spikes?
A: They're my armour. When a fox comes near, I dig straight down and leave only my spikes showing.
Q: What do you eat?
A: Ants and termites, mostly. I don't have teeth, so I catch them with my long, sticky tongue.
Q: Is it true you lay eggs?
A: It is. I lay one leathery egg and keep it in a pouch on my tummy until it hatches.
Q: What is a baby echidna called?
A: A puggle. It stays in my pouch until its spines start to grow, and then it's time to move out.
Q: And where do you live?
A: Almost anywhere in Australia, from the snowy mountains to the desert.
Q: Edna, thank you.
A: No worries. Mind the spikes on your way out.
encounters.prompt: How has the writer bent the usual shape of an animal report?
encounters.success: An interview. A host's questions, Edna's answers and a thank-you make it one, and the facts are all there.

options.text: The facts are sung as a song, with a chorus after each one.
options.reason: Nothing repeats like a chorus. It's questions and answers, like an interview.

options.text: The facts are given as answers in an interview with the echidna.

options.reason: There are no days or dates. Someone asks questions and Edna answers.

options.text: The facts are left out, and only the questions remain.
options.reason: Every question has an answer packed with facts: food, eggs and home.

encounters.text:
3 June. Arrived at dusk after a long climb. Lovely hut. Someone has left a candle burning in the window, which was kind. – Priya

5 June. Strange night. The candle was burning again when we arrived, but the hut was empty, and the logbook says Priya left two days ago. Who lit it? – Tom and Bec

7 June. Heard tapping in the walls all night. Tom thinks it's mice. I've hidden the chocolate. – Bec

9 June. Snowed in for two days. Each night the candle relit itself after we blew it out. Bec is sure it's a draught. I am sure it is not. – Tom

10 June. Bec has moved the chocolate twice. Still no sign of any mice. – Tom

12 June. Found the 'ghost'. A ringtail possum has been nesting in the wall behind the window. It knocks a box of matches onto the old heater every night, and the heat sets them smouldering. Mystery solved. Please, please fix the heater. – Ranger Kim

13 June. There is no heater in this hut. – Priya

parts: Every summer you come to visit me. You splash in my shallows, sail across my back and let your dogs chase my waves. I love the noise you make, and I love your sandcastles, even the ones that look like lumpy potatoes. But you leave things behind. Last week a turtle mistook a plastic bag for a jellyfish and nearly choked on it. A seal pup has been wearing a fishing net around its neck for a month. Every year, more of your bottles, wrappers and bottle caps wash into me, and they never really go away. They break into tiny pieces, smaller than grains of sand, and the fish swallow them.

encounters.frame: Mo reviewed the pie shop on the second tower for the Gazette. Indi wrote a note about it, and one word is wrong.
encounters.text:
My dearest Pie,
From the moment the waiter set you down in front of me, steaming and golden, I knew this was something special. I had smelled you three ladders below the shop, and I climbed faster than I have ever climbed. Your pastry was flaky, your gravy was rich, and your filling of beef and mushroom was hot all the way through, which is rare up here at two thousand metres. You cost only seven dollars, and you were worth every cent. The waiter was friendly, although he did give me a strange look when I started whispering to you. The only thing I did not love was the wait: twenty minutes in a queue that stretched out the door and onto the ledge. I am sorry I ate you so quickly. I will never forget you. You were the best thing I have eaten all year, and I have eaten a lot of things. I give you five stars out of five, and my whole heart. Next Saturday I will be back for your cousin, the apple pie. Please don't tell it about us.
Yours forever,
Mo

encounters.frame: Gus asked his robot to write up their science experiment. The Topsittle is reading the result.
encounters.text:
Gus asked his robot, Sprocket, to write up their science experiment as a report. Sprocket wrote a diary.

8:00 am. Gus says today we are finding out which melts ice fastest: salt, sugar or sand. Gus has given me a lab coat. It is too big. I am excited. I have never melted anything before, except a crayon, by accident.

8:15 am. We put three ice cubes of the same size on three plates. Gus sprinkled one spoon of salt on the first, one spoon of sugar on the second and one spoon of sand on the third. Gus says the plates must match and the room must stay the same temperature, or it isn't a fair test.

9:15 am. Results! The salty cube melted completely in 31 minutes. The sugary cube took 48 minutes. The sandy cube took 52 minutes, barely faster than a plain one. I timed them all with my internal clock, which is extremely accurate.

9:20 am. Conclusion: salt melts ice fastest. This is why people put salt on icy roads. Gus says I may write the next report too. I am honoured. He also says I should try pepper next time. I say pepper is for soup.
encounters.prompt: Sort these. What did Sprocket keep from a usual science report, and what did Sprocket change?
encounters.success: Sprocket kept the method, results and conclusion. The diary shape changed who is talking and how it is set out.

encounters.frame: The Scaffold Peaks gallery has a new sign about a famous island painter. The Topsittle has read it upside down.
encounters.text: At ninety, Mina Ostrova was the most famous painter on the island, and her mountain murals covered the walls of every school on Scaffold Peaks. Visitors came from all over the world to see them, and she still painted every morning before breakfast. Twenty years earlier, she had painted her greatest work, a sunrise over the towers so large it needed four ladders and a crane. Critics who had once ignored her called it a masterpiece. In her thirties, she had been almost unknown, selling small paintings of snow gums at the weekend market for five dollars each. Most weekends she sold none at all, and she lived on day-old bread. Before that, as a young woman, she had worked in a bakery, sketching customers on paper bags during her lunch break. Her boss once found a portrait of himself on a bag of bread rolls and hung it in the shop window. And it had all begun when she was seven, when her grandmother gave her a tin of watercolours and told her to paint whatever she could see from the kitchen window.
encounters.prompt: This biography runs from old age back to childhood. Why might the writer tell it that way?
encounters.success: Ending on a tin of watercolours shows how small Mina's start was, so her success feels even bigger.

options.text: To end on how small her start was, so her success feels bigger.
Because the writer forgot the order that her life happened in.
options.reason: Every step back is clear: twenty years earlier, her thirties, before that. It's backwards on purpose.

options.text: To make the biography shorter by leaving out her childhood.
options.reason: Her childhood is still there, at the very end: the tin of watercolours at seven.

options.text: To show that her early paintings were the best work she did.
options.reason: Critics called the later sunrise her masterpiece. Her early paintings hardly sold.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote the chairlift rules for the Scaffold Peaks ski school. The Topsittle rode the chairlift to read them.
encounters.text:
The Scaffold Peaks ski school asked Indi to write the chairlift rules for its youngest skiers. She wrote a fairy tale.

Once upon a time, a small skier named Pip came to the chairlift. A wise old wombat was waiting by the gate. 'Before you ride the magic chair,' said the wombat, 'you must learn three secrets.' The first secret was to wait behind the red line until the chair swung round behind you. The second was to sit right back and pull the safety bar down, snug across your tummy. The third, and most important, was never to wriggle, bounce or lean over to look at your boots, no matter how interesting they were. Pip learnt all three secrets. Up and up she floated, past the snow gums and the rock towers, until she reached the top. There she lifted the bar, stood up and skied away, as safe and happy as anyone had ever been. And every child who learns the wombat's secrets rides the magic chair safely, ever after.

The ski school has printed the story on a big sign beside the chairlift, with a picture of the wombat. Since then, not one small skier has wriggled.
encounters.prompt: Why did Indi turn the chairlift rules into a fairy tale?
encounters.success: Young children love stories. The wombat, the 'secrets' and the happy ending help the rules stick.

options.text: To teach young skiers about the wise wombats that live near the lift.
options.reason: The wombat only tells the rules. The story is about riding the chairlift safely.

options.text: To give older skiers something fun to read while they wait in the queue.
options.reason: The ski school asked for rules for its youngest skiers, not the older ones.

options.text: To make the rules easy for very young skiers to follow and remember.
Because the ski school asked her to write a story for its new sign.
options.reason: The ski school asked for chairlift rules. The fairy tale was Indi's own idea.
